content: 1. Pediatric Urology Guidelines: The 2011 guidelines on pediatric urology and the 2003 South African guidelines for managing nocturnal enuresis were excluded from analysis due to being outdated by more than two years. 2. Evidence-Based Treatments for Enuresis: Wespes (2010) reviewed enuresis treatments based on European Urological Association and International Children’s Continence Society guidelines but lacked systematic review methodology. 3. Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses: NICE (2010) conducted a more recent and rigorous systematic review and meta-analysis compared to earlier reviews by Glazener et al. (2008, 2009). NICE also provided GRADE evidence, focusing on psychological and social interventions for enuresis. 4. Fluid and Diet Restriction: NICE (2010) and Glazener (2009) included studies like Bhatia (1990) but found no data on symptom severity, functioning, or adverse effects. NICE (2010) remains the most comprehensive review but does not specifically address treatments within the first month of a traumatic event. 5. Behavioral Interventions: Lifting and Waking: This involves either lifting a sleeping child to urinate or waking them at set or random times. Six RCTs were reviewed, but no data on outcomes like symptom severity or adverse effects were reported. Bladder Training: This intervention aims to increase the interval between the urge to void and actual voiding. Five RCTs were included, but no outcome data were available. Star Charts: Reward systems for dry nights or correct toileting behavior were assessed in six RCTs. No data on symptom severity or adverse effects were reported. Dry Bed Training: This intensive program includes positive practice, fluid intake at bedtime, alarms, and cleanliness training. Five RCTs were reviewed, but no data on outcomes were available. 6. Enuresis Alarms: Alarms triggered by urine contact were evaluated in 10 RCTs. These devices can produce sounds or vibrations. NICE (2010) found moderate-quality evidence suggesting clinical benefit, but no data on functioning or adverse effects were reported. 7. Psychological Interventions: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT): Only one study compared CBT to no treatment. The evidence was of low quality, with minimal to clinically appreciable benefit reported. Other Psychological Treatments: Limited evidence exists, with only head-to-head comparisons available. 8. Educational Interventions: No studies compared information and educational interventions to no treatment or control conditions. 9. Alternative Treatments (e.g., Hypnosis): No studies compared hypnosis to no treatment or control conditions. 10. Quality of Evidence: Many studies included in the analyses had significant limitations, such as high dropout rates, unclear allocation concealment, lack of blinding, and small sample sizes. Confidence intervals often ranged from no benefit to potential harm or benefit. 11. Clinical Guidelines: NICE (2010) provided comprehensive clinical guidelines based on systematic reviews of pharmacological and psychological interventions. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing active treatments to usual care or control conditions were included in GRADE tables. 12. Practical Considerations: Families often attempt fluid restriction before seeking professional help. Children with bedwetting may also restrict fluids during the day to manage symptoms of urgency and frequency. Dietary restrictions are hypothesized to help based on the idea that food allergies may provoke bladder instability. 13. Definitions and Descriptions: Lifting: Moving a sleeping child to urinate without waking them. Waking: Actively waking a child to urinate, either at set or random times. Dry Bed Training: A structured program involving alarms, waking routines, and positive reinforcement. Enuresis Alarms: Battery-powered devices that alert the child when urination begins. 14. Limitations of Evidence: Many studies failed to report standard deviations, had small sample sizes, or lacked baseline comparability. Some studies did not explicitly exclude children with physical causes of enuresis.
